title: Teaching LLMs to Recommend and Defer in Underrepresented Epilepsy Care
claim: A learning loop turns supervised errors into evolving shared memory, whose trajectory is ensembled at inference to give predictions and deferral.
layout: 2 panels, left adaptation and right deployment, top-to-bottom flows, color-coded agent boxes
description: Two panels split by a dashed vertical line. Panel A, 'Adaptation on medical records', has a pink region where patient records (x_i, x_j, x_k) flow left to right into a cyan Predictor robot box, which outputs 3 drug regimens. These go to a cyan Inspector box with a magnifier icon, which outputs report-plus-learnings c_i, c_j, c_k into a cylinder, the shared candidate-learnings buffer. An arrow leads down to a cream Architect box, then to a purple 'Updated state m_t' box. That box shows two forms: Single (a rule list with Add and None actions) and Multi (specialist prompts with Spawn, Edit, Prune and None actions). Panel B, 'Deployment on new cases', runs top to bottom. A new patient feeds a memory trajectory m0..mT, then a Bayesian prompt average box, then a probability bar chart over regimens. The chart splits into a green high-confidence branch (assist clinician) and a red low-confidence branch (refer to specialist).
caption: \learnmethod{} workflow. (A) During adaptation, each batch of patient records is processed with the current memory state: the Predictor proposes three regimens, the Inspector compares them with the physician prescription revealed as supervision, and the proposed candidate learnings accumulate in an append-only buffer. Once per batch, the Architect consolidates recurring cross-case signals into the next shared memory, either as a Single correction-rule list or a Multi specialist-prompt population. (B) At inference, the learned memory trajectory is treated as an ensemble of prompt states. Bayesian prompt averaging converts their candidate regimen predictions into prescription probabilities, enabling high-confidence assistance or deferral to a specialist.
abstract: Specialist epilepsy expertise is scarce in resource-constrained settings. Clinical decision-support systems must adapt to local prescribing practices and recognize when specialist review is needed. We study pediatric epilepsy care in Uganda, predicting anti-seizure medication regimens from longitudinal clinic notes. General-purpose language models achieve non-trivial agreement with physician prescriptions, but neurologists' review reveals Western prescribing defaults that do not account for local practices. We introduce MANANA, a non-parametric prompt-learning framework that learns local prescribing guidance from a small patient-level training set. MANANA turns prescription errors into auditable prompt memory, with single-agent and multi-agent variants, and improves over classical ML models, direct LLM prompting, and prompt-optimization baselines across two independently collected Ugandan cohorts. The learned prompt trajectory also provides a basis for estimating uncertainty. Bayesian prompt averaging (BPA) combines predictions across this trajectory to produce prescription likelihoods and a deferral signal. Using the same MANANA-Multi trajectory, BPA improves top-1 physician-regimen agreement from 66% to 70% on Cohort A and from 73% to 75% on Cohort B while preserving top-3 coverage. On Cohort B, its most confident half of cases achieves 95% precision, and its most confident quarter achieves 99% precision, supporting deferral of lower-confidence cases for specialist review. These results suggest a path toward locally adapted clinical LLM systems that learn from limited site-specific data and focus scarce specialist attention on uncertain cases.
